paragraphs: I am not a doctor, but I feel the time has come when I must give the reader some account of Ivan’s illness. I can tell you one thing in advance: at that moment he was on the very eve of an attack of brain fever. His health had been poor for a long time, but it had put up a stubborn resistance to the fever, which in the end overpowered it. I know nothing of medicine, but I will risk a guess. By a terrible effort of will he had perhaps managed to hold the attack off for a while, hoping, of course, to stop it altogether. He knew he was unwell. But he hated the thought of being ill at that fatal time, at the approaching crisis of his life, when he needed all his wits about him, to say what he had to say boldly and firmly and “to justify himself to himself.”

He had, however, gone to see the new doctor, the one brought from Moscow on Katerina Ivanovna’s fantastic notion, which I have mentioned already. The doctor listened to him and examined him. He concluded that Ivan really was suffering from some disorder of the brain, and he was not at all surprised by an admission Ivan had made him reluctantly. “Hallucinations are quite likely in your condition,” the doctor said, “though it would be better to check them ... You must take steps at once, without losing a moment, or things will go badly for you.” But Ivan did not follow this sensible advice and did not take to his bed to be nursed. “I’m walking about, so I’m strong enough. If I drop, it will be different. Then anyone who likes can nurse me,” he decided, and dismissed the subject.

And so he sat there, almost aware of his own delirium and, as I have said already, staring fixedly at something on the sofa against the opposite wall. Someone seemed to be sitting there, though goodness knows how he had come in, for he had not been in the room when Ivan entered it on his return from Smerdyakov. This was a man, or more exactly a Russian gentleman of a particular kind, no longer young, _qui faisait la cinquantaine_, as the French say. His dark hair was rather long and still thick, slightly streaked with gray, and he had a small pointed beard. He wore a brownish reefer jacket, rather shabby, though evidently made by a good tailor. It was in a style at least three years old, one that smart and well-to-do people had dropped for the last two years. His linen and his long scarf-like necktie were the kind worn by people who aim at looking stylish, but on closer inspection the linen was not very clean and the wide scarf was badly worn. The visitor’s check trousers were excellently cut, but too light in color and too tight for the present fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat did not suit the season.

In short, he had every look of gentility on straitened means. He seemed to belong to the class of idle landowners who flourished in the days of serfdom. He had unmistakably been in good, fashionable society at one time and had once had good connections, and he had possibly kept them. But after a gay youth he had been gradually impoverished by the abolition of serfdom, and he had sunk into the position of a poor relation of the best sort. He wandered from one good old friend to another. They received him for his companionable and accommodating nature and because he was, after all, a gentleman who could be asked to sit down with anyone, though not, of course, in the place of honor. Such accommodating gentlemen in dependent positions, who can tell a story and take a hand at cards, and who strongly dislike any duties forced on them, are usually solitary creatures, either bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but then the children are always being brought up at a distance, at some aunt’s, whom these gentlemen never mention in good society, as if ashamed of the relationship. Little by little they lose sight of their children altogether, though now and then they get a birthday or Christmas letter from them and sometimes even answer it.

The face of the unexpected visitor was not so much good-natured as accommodating, ready to take on any amiable expression as the occasion required. He had no watch, but he had a tortoise-shell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand he wore a massive gold ring with a cheap opal in it.

Ivan was angrily silent and would not begin the conversation. The visitor waited. He sat exactly like a poor relation who had come down from his room to keep his host company at tea, and who was discreetly silent because his host was frowning and preoccupied. But he was ready for any friendly conversation as soon as his host should start it. All at once his face showed sudden concern.

“I say,” he began, turning to Ivan, “excuse me, I only mention it to remind you. You went to Smerdyakov’s to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, but you came away without learning anything about her. You probably forgot—”

“Ah, yes,” broke from Ivan, and his face grew dark with uneasiness. “Yes, I’d forgotten ... but it doesn’t matter now, never mind, it can wait till tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. “And you,” he added, turning to his visitor, “I’d have remembered it myself in a minute, for that was just what was tormenting me! Why do you interfere, as if I’d believe you prompted me and I didn’t remember it myself?”

“Don’t believe it, then,” said the gentleman, smiling amiably. “What’s the good of believing against your will? Besides, proofs are no help to belief, especially material proofs. Thomas believed, not because he saw Christ risen, but because he wanted to believe, before he saw. Look at the spiritualists, for instance ... I’m very fond of them ... just imagine, they think they’re serving the cause of religion because the devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, that another world exists. The other world and material proofs, what next! And if you come to that, does proving there’s a devil prove there’s a God? I want to join an idealist society. I’ll lead the opposition in it. I’ll say I’m a realist but not a materialist, he he!”

“Listen,” Ivan said, suddenly getting up from the table. “I seem to be delirious ... I am delirious, in fact. Talk any nonsense you like, I don’t care! You won’t drive me to fury, as you did last time. But I feel somehow ashamed ... I want to walk about the room ... Sometimes I don’t see you and don’t even hear your voice, as I did last time, but I always guess what you’re prattling, because it’s _I myself speaking, not you_. Only I don’t know whether I was dreaming last time or whether I really saw you. I’ll wet a towel and put it on my head, and perhaps you’ll vanish into thin air.”
Ivan went to the corner, took a towel, and did as he had said. With the wet towel on his head he began walking up and down the room.
“I’m so glad you treat me so familiarly,” the visitor began.

“Fool,” Ivan laughed, “do you think I’d stand on ceremony with you? I’m in good spirits now, though I have a pain in my forehead ... and in the top of my head ... Only please don’t talk philosophy, as you did last time. If you can’t take yourself off, talk about something amusing. Tell me gossip. You’re a poor relation, you ought to talk gossip. What a nightmare to have! But I’m not afraid of you. I’ll get the better of you. I won’t be taken to a madhouse!”

“_C’est charmant_, poor relation. Yes, I’m in my natural shape. For what am I on earth but a poor relation? By the way, I’m listening to you and I’m rather surprised to find you’re actually beginning to take me for something real, and not just your fancy, as you insisted last time—”

“Not for one minute have I taken you for real,” Ivan cried with a sort of fury. “You’re a lie, you’re my illness, you’re a phantom. It’s only that I don’t know how to destroy you, and I see I must suffer for a time. You’re my hallucination. You’re the incarnation of myself, but only of one side of me ... of my thoughts and feelings, but only the nastiest and stupidest of them. From that point of view you might interest me, if only I had time to waste on you—”

“Excuse me, excuse me, I’ll catch you out. When you flew at Alyosha under the lamp-post this evening and shouted to him, ‘You learned it from _him_! How do you know that _he_ visits me?’ you were thinking of me then. So for one brief moment you did believe that I really exist,” the gentleman laughed blandly.
“Yes, that was a moment of weakness ... but I couldn’t believe in you. I don’t know whether I was asleep or awake last time. Perhaps I was only dreaming then and didn’t see you at all—”
“And why were you so surly with Alyosha just now? He’s a dear. I’ve treated him badly over Father Zossima.”
“Don’t talk about Alyosha! How dare you, you flunkey!” Ivan laughed again.
“You scold me, but you laugh, and that’s a good sign. But you’re ever so much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours—”
“Don’t speak of my resolution,” Ivan cried savagely.
“I understand, I understand, _c’est noble, c’est charmant_, you’re going to defend your brother and sacrifice yourself ... _C’est chevaleresque_.”
“Hold your tongue, or I’ll kick you!”

“I won’t be altogether sorry, because then my object will be achieved. If you kick me, you must believe I’m real, since people don’t kick ghosts. Joking aside, it makes no difference to me. Scold if you like, though it’s better to be a little more polite, even to me. ‘Fool, flunkey!’ What words!”
“When I scold you, I scold myself,” Ivan laughed again. “You are myself, myself, only with a different face. You just say what I’m thinking ... and you’re incapable of saying anything new!”
“If I’m like you in the way I think, that’s all to my credit,” the gentleman declared, with delicacy and dignity.

“You pick out only my worst thoughts, and what’s more, the stupid ones. You’re stupid and vulgar. You’re awfully stupid. No, I can’t put up with you! What am I to do, what am I to do?” Ivan said through clenched teeth.

“My dear friend, above all I want to behave like a gentleman and to be recognized as one,” the visitor began, in an excess of apologetic, simple-hearted pride, typical of a poor relation. “I’m poor, but ... I won’t say very honest, but ... it’s an axiom generally accepted in society that I’m a fallen angel. I certainly can’t conceive how I can ever have been an angel. If I ever was, it must have been so long ago that there’s no harm in forgetting it. Now I only prize my reputation as a gentlemanly person, and I live as I can, trying to make myself agreeable. I love men genuinely, I’ve been greatly slandered! When I stay with you from time to time here, my life gains a kind of reality, and that’s what I like most of all. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastic, and so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything is bounded, here all is formulated and geometrical, while we have nothing but indeterminate equations! I wander about here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I become superstitious. Please don’t laugh, that’s just what I like, to become superstitious. I adopt all your habits here: I’ve grown fond of going to the public baths, would you believe it? I go and steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once for all and irrevocably in the form of some merchant’s wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing all she believes. My ideal is to go to church and offer a candle in simple-hearted faith, upon my word it is. Then there would be an end to my sufferings. I like being doctored too. In the spring there was an outbreak of smallpox, and I went and was vaccinated in a foundling hospital. If only you knew how I enjoyed myself that day! I gave ten roubles to the cause of the Slavs! ... But you’re not listening. Do you know, you’re not at all well this evening? I know you went to that doctor yesterday ... well, how is your health? What did the doctor say?”
“Fool!” Ivan snapped out.
“But you’re clever, anyway. You’re scolding again? I didn’t ask out of sympathy. You needn’t answer. Now the rheumatism has come back—”
“Fool!” Ivan repeated.
“You keep saying the same thing, but I had such an attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this day.”
“The devil have rheumatism!”
“Why not, if I sometimes put on fleshly form? I put on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”
“What, what, Satan _sum et nihil humanum_ ... that’s not bad for the devil!”
“I’m glad I’ve pleased you at last.”
“But you didn’t get that from me.” Ivan stopped suddenly, as if struck. “That never entered my head. That’s strange.”

“_C’est du nouveau, n’est-ce pas?_ This time I’ll act honestly and explain it to you. Listen. In dreams, and especially in nightmares, from indigestion or anything else, a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such complex and real actuality, such events, even a whole world of events, woven into such a plot, with such unexpected details, from the most exalted matters down to the last button on a cuff, as I swear Leo Tolstoy has never invented. Yet such dreams are sometimes seen not by writers but by the most ordinary people, officials, journalists, priests ... The whole subject is a complete enigma. A statesman actually confessed to me that all his best ideas came to him when he was asleep. Well, that’s how it is now. Though I’m your hallucination, yet just as in a nightmare I say original things that had not entered your head before. So I don’t repeat your ideas, and yet I’m only your nightmare, nothing more.”
“You’re lying. Your aim is to convince me that you exist apart and are not my nightmare, and now you’re claiming you’re a dream.”
“My dear fellow, I’ve adopted a special method today, I’ll explain it to you afterwards. Wait, where did I leave off? Oh, yes! I caught cold then, only not here but over there.”

“Where is over there? Tell me, will you be here long? Can’t you go away?” Ivan exclaimed almost in despair. He stopped walking to and fro, sat down on the sofa, leaned his elbows on the table again and held his head tight in both hands. He pulled off the wet towel and flung it away in vexation. It was evidently of no use.
